text:
## Observations

1. The empty path gives distance 0 from each vertex to itself, and every directed edge gives a palindrome of length 1.
2. Every palindrome of length at least 2 has matching first and last labels, and removing those two edges leaves a shorter palindromic path.
3. A matching pair of outer edges can be added in two unit-cost steps if an intermediate state remembers the label that must be matched.
4. A FIFO breadth-first search with all distance-0 seeds queued before all distance-1 seeds processes states in nondecreasing distance order.
5. Only completed palindrome states correspond to answers; a completed state that is never reached has answer -1.
6. If the graph has M edges, each edge can generate at most N transitions of each of the two extension types.

## Solution sketch

> The empty path gives distance 0 from each vertex to itself, and every directed edge gives a palindrome of length 1.

1. Store incoming edges for each vertex and group outgoing edges by source and label, ignoring `-` entries. Use a completed state \((u,v)\) for a palindromic path from \(u\) to \(v\). Initialize every diagonal state to distance 0 and enqueue them first. Then initialize and enqueue each still-unvisited state with a direct edge at distance 1. In particular, a self-loop does not replace a diagonal answer of 0.

> Every palindrome of length at least 2 has matching first and last labels, and removing those two edges leaves a shorter palindromic path.

2. Grow palindromes outward from the seeds: from a completed state \((u,v)\), an edge \(a\to u\) and an edge \(v\to b\) with the same label produce a palindrome from \(a\) to \(b\). This operation produces only palindromes, and repeated removal of matching outer edges shows that it can generate every palindromic path from an empty or single-edge center.

> A matching pair of outer edges can be added in two unit-cost steps if an intermediate state remembers the label that must be matched.

3. Implement the outward extension without enumerating pairs of edges. From \((u,v)\), each incoming edge \(a\to u\) labeled \(c\) leads to the pending state \((a,v,c)\). From that pending state, each outgoing edge \(v\to b\) labeled \(c\) leads to the completed state \((a,b)\). Each transition costs 1. The pending state need not retain \(u\), since the valid continuations depend only on \(v\) and \(c\), and all of them produce the same respective endpoints \(a,b\).

> A FIFO breadth-first search with all distance-0 seeds queued before all distance-1 seeds processes states in nondecreasing distance order.

4. Process both state types in one FIFO queue. When a transition reaches an unvisited state, assign it the current distance plus 1 and enqueue it. Expanding distance-0 states can append only distance-1 states, so the initial queue order is preserved; from then on, ordinary unit-cost BFS applies. First discovery therefore gives the shortest distance to each state. Marking states on discovery also keeps cycles from causing repeated work.

> Only completed palindrome states correspond to answers; a completed state that is never reached has answer -1.

5. Print the completed-state distances in vertex-pair order, using \(-1\) for unvisited pairs. If there are no edges, only the diagonal states are reached, so the same procedure handles that case as well.

> If the graph has M edges, each edge can generate at most N transitions of each of the two extension types.

6. Generate transitions on demand. A left edge can be scanned once per right endpoint \(v\), and a right edge can be scanned once per left endpoint \(a\) in a pending state with its label. With a fixed alphabet of 26 letters, there are \(O(N^2)\) states. Including input and output, the total time is \(O(N^2+NM)\), or \(O(N^3)\) in the dense case, and the space usage is \(O(N^2)\).
